adventure.title: Fort Henry Living History, Kingston
adventure.description: The 1830s British fortification on the limestone headland above Kingston does living history performances with uniforms, cannon fire, and soldiers drilling — the fort controls the entire St. Lawrence approach.
adventure.bonus: Stay for the sunset retreat ceremony with cannon salute.

adventure.title: Kayak the Admiralty Islands Group
adventure.description: The cluster of state park islands in the American Narrows — Murray, Calumet, Wellesley Island — are connected by paddling routes through protected channels that cut you off from the river current.
adventure.bonus: Paddle the entire channel loop without stopping on any island until you've completed it.

adventure.title: Muskie Fishing the International Section
adventure.description: The St. Lawrence International section between the islands produces the largest muskie in North America — hire a guide in Clayton or Alexandria Bay, use big bucktails, and hang on.
adventure.bonus: Catch and release — the muskie fishery exists because of catch-and-release.

adventure.title: St. Lawrence River Scuba Wreck Dive
adventure.description: The St. Lawrence has over 200 documented shipwrecks visible in its cold, clear water — the Robert Gaskin and the Keystorm both sit in 60 feet of water with intact hulls. The freshwater visibility is 30+ feet.
adventure.bonus: Dive the Keystorm — the steel freighter sits upright on the bottom with its superstructure intact.

adventure.title: Seaway Trail Scenic Drive — Cape Vincent to Alexandria Bay
adventure.description: The 30-mile drive on the Seaway Trail along the American shore from Cape Vincent to Alexandria Bay passes every lighthouse, river access, and castle view on the US side — stop at every pull-off.
adventure.bonus: Stop at every river access point and take a photo of the same view at different times of day.

adventure.title: Island-Hopping by Pontoon Boat
adventure.description: Rent a pontoon for the day and navigate the 1,864 islands yourself — through the American Narrows, past the castles, into the back channels where the osprey fish and the current runs cold.
adventure.bonus: Find an uninhabited island, tie up, and swim off the rocks.

active.title: Canoe the Back Channels at Dawn
active.description: The narrow channels between the smaller islands are only navigable by canoe or kayak — blue herons fish the shallows at dawn, bass hold in the lily pads, and the river traffic hasn't started yet.
active.bonus: Get on the water before 6am — the mist on the river channels at dawn is the whole thing.

active.title: Wellesley Island State Park Trail System
active.description: The 2,636-acre state park has 10 miles of hiking and biking trails through old-growth forest and along the river shore — the Eel Bay trail leads to a secluded rocky beach accessible only on foot.
active.bonus: Find the Eel Bay beach at the end of the trail and swim.

active.title: Sunrise Run — Thousand Islands Bridge Span
active.description: The annual Seaway Run lets you run across the Thousand Islands Bridge spans — the rest of the year you can drive across and park at Hill Island for a run along the Canadian shore with the bridge visible upstream.
active.bonus: Run to the midpoint of the bridge and stop to look at the river below — you can see the current splitting around the islands.

active.title: Kayak Circumnavigation of Wellesley Island
active.description: The full circumnavigation of Wellesley Island by kayak is 18 miles through island channels, past state park campgrounds, under the Thousand Islands Bridge, and back to the put-in — a full day on the water.
active.bonus: Camp overnight on the island and finish the second half the next morning.

active.title: Walleye Fishing Charter, Clayton Marina
active.description: The Clayton fishing charters run the international section for walleye from May through October — drift-jigging the rock structures in 20 feet of water at dawn with a guide who's fished this stretch for 30 years.
active.bonus: Keep two walleye and cook them that night — that's the point.

active.title: Seaway Trail Bike Ride — River Road
active.description: The Seaway Trail bike route from Cape Vincent east follows the river at water level — low traffic, river views on the left, farmland on the right, the Canadian shore visible across the current.
active.bonus: Bike the full section without earphones — the river sounds change at every inlet.

active.title: Stand-Up Paddleboard Between Islands
active.description: The protected channels between the islands are ideal for SUP on calm mornings — the water clarity is 15+ feet, the current in the back channels is manageable, and no boat wake gets through.
active.bonus: Paddle over the clearest water you can find and look at the bottom.

active.title: Swim Off the Rocks on a Private Island
active.description: The St. Lawrence runs 60–70 degrees in July with visibility to 20 feet — find a state park island, tie your boat, climb the granite rocks, and jump. There is no better swimming in New York.
active.bonus: Find a rock that drops directly into 10 feet of clear water and use it until sunset.

social.title: Sackets Harbor Brewpub Night
social.description: The small Lake Ontario harbor town has a brewpub in the historic district with the harbor visible from the bar — cold pints, the battlefield two blocks away, and a summer night that goes quiet by 10.
social.bonus: Walk to the harbor after last call and sit on the dock until midnight.

social.title: Dockside Pub, Gananoque Waterfront
social.description: The Gananoque waterfront pub with live music on weekends and a deck that hangs over the marina — cold Molson, fish and chips, and the Canadian side of the river doing exactly what summer should do.
social.bonus: Stay for the full set of whoever's playing and buy them a drink after.

social.title: Sunset Dinner Cruise on the St. Lawrence
social.description: The two-hour dinner cruise from Alexandria Bay or Gananoque threads through the island channels as the sun drops behind the Canadian shore — the islands glow orange and the river turns pink.
social.bonus: Stand at the bow for the full sunset — don't stay at the dinner table for it.

social.title: Bonnie Castle Resort River Bar
social.description: The Alexandria Bay resort bar on the river with Boldt Castle across the water — the patio fills at sunset with people who've been on the water all day and have exactly nowhere to be tomorrow.
social.bonus: Watch the last boat pass Boldt Castle before the lights come on.

social.title: Thousand Islands Brewing, Clayton
social.description: The Clayton craft brewery does a River Water IPA and a Summer Ale that both make sense when you're sitting on the dock after a day on the water.
social.bonus: Order the sampler flight and rank every beer.

social.title: Island Bonfire Night — Private Rental Island
social.description: Several of the smaller Thousand Islands are available for overnight rental through NY State Parks — camp on your own island, build a fire on the rock shore, watch the river traffic with a cold beer.
social.bonus: Stay awake long enough to see the stars over the river — there's almost no light pollution.

social.title: Kingston Pub Crawl — Princess Street
social.description: Kingston's Princess Street has the densest concentration of bars and live music west of Montreal — the university town energy means the bars are good and the crowd is actually interesting.
social.bonus: Hit at least five different bars on the same block without repeating.

social.title: Boldt Castle Night Tour, Heart Island
social.description: George Boldt's uncompleted 120-room castle on Heart Island runs evening boat tours that put you on the island after the day crowds leave — the stone towers, the power house, the river at dusk.
social.bonus: Read the story of Boldt and his wife Louise before you go — the castle is a love story.

chill.title: Fort Wellington National Historic Site
chill.description: The 1812-era British fort in Prescott, Ontario is one of the best-preserved military sites in Canada — the blockhouse, the defensive earthworks, and the view across the river to Ogdensburg, NY.
chill.bonus: Find the spot where you can see both the American and Canadian shores simultaneously.

chill.title: Zavikon Island — World's Shortest International Bridge
chill.description: The 32-foot footbridge connecting two islands — one American, one Canadian — is the world's shortest international bridge. You need a boat to get there. It's worth it for the sheer absurdity alone.
chill.bonus: Cross the bridge three times, stepping into a different country each time.

chill.title: Wolfe Island Ferry + Sunset Walk
chill.description: The free ferry from Kingston to Wolfe Island takes 20 minutes and drops you on the largest of the Thousand Islands — flat farmland, wind turbines, a general store, and the river visible from every road.
chill.bonus: Bike or walk to the island's south shore and watch the ferry cross at sunset.

chill.title: Boldt Castle Full Exploration, Heart Island
chill.description: George Boldt stopped construction in 1904 when his wife died and left 120 rooms unfinished for 73 years — the Thousand Islands Bridge Authority has been restoring it since 1977. Take the boat, take your time.
chill.bonus: Find the Alster Tower playhouse on the back island and climb to the top.

chill.title: Rock Island Lighthouse Boat Tour
chill.description: The 1847 lighthouse on Rock Island at the head of the Chippewa Bay has been restored and is open for tours by boat — the view from the top across the American channel is the whole Thousand Islands in one glance.
chill.bonus: Climb the lighthouse stairs to the lamp room — count the islands you can identify by name.

chill.title: Singer Castle on Dark Island
chill.description: The 1905 castle on Dark Island was built for the Singer sewing machine heir and has underground tunnels, a dungeon, and a priest hole — guided tours only, absolutely worth it.
chill.bonus: Ask the guide to show you the tunnel system — it goes under the island.

chill.title: Antique Boat Museum, Clayton
chill.description: The Clayton museum has the world's largest freshwater antique boat collection — Gilded Age mahogany runabouts, St. Lawrence skiffs, and the 1923 houseboat La Duchesse that was never finished.
chill.bonus: Find the oldest boat in the collection and read its entire history card.

chill.title: Kingston's Limestone District Walk
chill.description: Kingston's entire downtown is built in 19th-century limestone — City Hall, Martello towers, Fort Henry, the waterfront market — the most historically intact city on the Great Lakes.
chill.bonus: Walk to the Martello tower at Murney Point and look back at the city from the lake.

foodie.title: Kingston Public Market, Ontario
foodie.description: The Kingston Farmers' Market has operated since 1801 in Springer Market Square — local cheese, Ontario produce, maple syrup, and the best butter tarts you will ever eat.
foodie.bonus: Buy butter tarts from at least three different vendors and compare.

foodie.title: Fresh Walleye Dinner at a Riverside Camp
foodie.description: The St. Lawrence runs the finest walleye fishery on the continent — catch them yourself or buy direct from a guide, pan-fry in butter with Old Bay, eat on a dock with the river moving past.
foodie.bonus: Cook them outside, eat them outside, don't go inside until dark.

foodie.title: Cavallario's Steak & Seafood, Alexandria Bay
foodie.description: The waterfront institution in Alexandria Bay with Boldt Castle visible from the dining room — the walleye and the prime rib have been the move here since before anyone living can remember.
foodie.bonus: Get a window table and watch the tour boats go past Boldt Castle during dinner.

foodie.title: Otter's Lakehouse, Clayton
foodie.description: The casual waterfront bar and grill in Clayton with the best deck view of the river — the fish tacos and the cold draft in a plastic cup on the dock is the whole summer in one order.
foodie.bonus: Arrive by boat if possible — dock at the marina and walk up.

foodie.title: Riverhouse Restaurant on the Gananoque
foodie.description: The Gananoque restaurant perched on the river bank with the best Ontario lamb and the most extensive local wine list on the Canadian side of the river.
foodie.bonus: Order the Ontario lamb and a bottle of Prince Edward County Pinot Noir.

foodie.title: Thousand Islands Winery, Cape Vincent
foodie.description: The Cape Vincent winery on the shore of the St. Lawrence makes cold-climate wines from Niagara grapes with a tasting room overlooking the river — the ice wine and the Frontenac red are the keepers.
foodie.bonus: Buy a bottle of the ice wine and drink it that night watching the river.

foodie.title: The Original Thousand Island Dressing Location
foodie.description: The dressing was created in the early 1900s by Sophie Lalonde, a fishing guide's wife on the river, and served at the Boldt Hotel on Wellesley Island — order it at any local restaurant and tell the story.
foodie.bonus: Order it on something that doesn't normally come with dressing.

foodie.title: Sackets Harbor Battlefield Tavern Dinner
foodie.description: The restaurant in the 1817 tavern building overlooking the Sackets Harbor battlefield and Lake Ontario serves exactly the kind of dinner that belongs here: roast chicken, local vegetables, cold beer.
foodie.bonus: Walk the battlefield after dinner while it's still light.

foodie.title: Koffee Kove Diner, Clayton Waterfront
foodie.description: The Clayton waterfront diner with booths facing the river and a breakfast menu that hasn't changed in 30 years — the French toast and the egg sandwich are the order of everyone who's been coming here since childhood.
foodie.bonus: Sit at the counter and talk to whoever's there — they'll know everyone.

foodie.title: Gananoque Inn Waterfront Dinner
foodie.description: The historic inn on the Gananoque River a block from the St. Lawrence does a waterfront dinner on the patio — the best table in Gananoque on a summer evening, local fish, Ontario wine.
foodie.bonus: Reserve the patio table closest to the river — the Gananoque flows past three feet away.
